content: Gaucher disease is the most prevalent lysosomal storage disorder, caused by a deficiency in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Current treatment options for this condition include enzyme replacement therapy, substrate reduction therapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). HSCT is a high-risk medical procedure, but it may offer long-term benefits, particularly in reversing skeletal and neurological complications associated with Gaucher disease. This document represents an updated version of a previously published Cochrane Review. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the role of HSCT in individuals with Gaucher disease. Specifically, it aimed to assess the mortality risks associated with the procedure, its effectiveness in altering the progression of the disease, and its ability to halt or reverse neurological symptoms in neuronopathic forms of the disease (types 2 and 3). To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted within the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register. This register includes references obtained from extensive electronic database searches and manual reviews of pertinent journals and conference abstracts. The most recent search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was performed on January 19, 2017. Additionally, searches were conducted on clinical trial websites, including ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and Genzyme Clinical Research, with the latest search completed on March 2, 2017. The selection criteria for this review included all randomized, quasi-randomized, and controlled clinical trials that compared HSCT with enzyme replacement therapy, substrate reduction therapy, symptomatic treatment, or no treatment in individuals of any age diagnosed with Gaucher disease. Despite an independent assessment of trials for inclusion, no relevant trials were identified. A total of 32 trials were identified through the search process. However, none of these trials met the criteria for inclusion in the review. Consequently, no data were available for analysis. The authors concluded that HSCT has the potential to provide a permanent cure for Gaucher disease. However, there is currently no clinical trial evidence to evaluate the safety and efficacy of HSCT compared to other established treatments, such as enzyme replacement therapy and substrate reduction therapy. As no relevant trials were identified up to March 2017, the authors do not plan to update this review until new clinical trials are published.
